Rate choropleth map (numerator per denominator)

Source: R/rate_choropleth_map.R
mysterymaps_rate_choropleth_map.Rd

Shades each polygon by a rate – numerator_var / denominator_var * per – rather than a raw count, so a reader compares areas fairly instead of larger-population areas simply looking darker.

Usage

mysterymaps_rate_choropleth_map(
  polygons,
  numerator_var,
  denominator_var,
  numerator_label,
  denominator_label,
  per = 1e+05,
  title = NULL,
  subtitle = NULL,
  caption = NULL,
  k = 6,
  digits = 1,
  zero_color = "#e0e0e0",
  na_color = "#ffffff",
  viridis_option = "viridis",
  crs = 5070
)

Arguments

polygons

sf polygon layer.

numerator_var, denominator_var

character(1): numeric columns in polygons.

numerator_label, denominator_label

character(1): full-word labels used to build the legend title.

per

numeric(1): rate denominator scale, e.g. 100000 for "per 100,000". Default 100000.

title, subtitle, caption

Character labels. NULL omits.

k

integer(1): target number of Jenks classes for the positive rates, passed to mysterymaps_jenks_zero_scale(). Default 6.

digits

integer(1): decimal places in the legend's rate labels. Default 1; pass 0 when the rate reads more naturally as a whole number (e.g. "per 1,000" counts that are rarely fractional in practice).

zero_color, na_color

Colours for a measured-zero rate and for an undefined (zero-denominator) rate, respectively. Defaults match mysterymaps_jenks_zero_scale()'s own.

viridis_option

character(1): passed to the option argument of the viridisLite::viridis() palette used for the positive classes.

crs

Projection for display. Default EPSG:5070 (Albers Equal Area), appropriate for the contiguous United States.

Value

A ggplot object. The caller saves it; this function writes nothing.

Details

This function takes polygons with both variables already attached and does no joining itself. That is deliberate: in at least one prior use of this pattern (Virginia counties), joining a rate's two halves by the NAME column silently merged the wrong rows, because Fairfax, Franklin, Richmond, and Roanoke each name both a county AND a same-named independent city. Push any such join to the caller, and join by a stable identifier (e.g. GEOID), never by a place name.

The legend title is always built from numerator_label and denominator_label in full words – pass "Urogynecologists" and "Women Age 40 and Older", not "Urogyn" and "W40+" – because this title is the one place in the map an abbreviation would otherwise land by default.

Zero is a category, not the bottom of a gradient

An earlier version of this function coloured the rate with a plain continuous scale_fill_viridis_c() (optionally log1p-transformed for skew). That repeats, on a brand-new function, the exact mistake mysterymaps_jenks_zero_scale() exists to prevent: a polygon with a measured rate of zero (real population, no provider) rendered identically to one just barely above zero, both near the dark end of the gradient – on a prior national map this put over half the counties in the country into one indistinguishable "low" class when the honest answer for most of them was "none". This function now classifies .mm_rate with mysterymaps_jenks_zero_scale() instead: zero gets its own colour and legend entry, positive rates are Jenks-classified (which is also why there is no log_scale argument any more – natural breaks already handle the right-skewed distribution a log transform was compensating for), and a polygon with a zero denominator (.mm_rate is NA, an undefined rate, not a measured one) gets na_color rather than being folded into the zero class.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # interactive()
counties <- sf::st_sf(
  n_providers = c(1, 2, 0, 4),
  population = c(10000, 100000, 50000, 200000),
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(lapply(1:4, function(i) {
    x <- -100 + i
    sf::st_polygon(list(cbind(c(x, x + 1, x + 1, x, x), c(40, 40, 41, 41, 40))))
  }), crs = 4326)
)
mysterymaps_rate_choropleth_map(
  counties, numerator_var = "n_providers", denominator_var = "population",
  numerator_label = "Urogynecologists", denominator_label = "Women Age 40 and Older")
}
